core: Working definition of infancy: the period from birth to about age two (NICHD)
Rapid physical growth and change during the first two years
Motor milestones as typical ranges with variation: rolling, sitting, crawling, walking (CDC, MedlinePlus)
Sensory development in infancy: hearing, vision, touch (MedlinePlus, CDC)
Piaget's sensorimotor stage as the cognitive hallmark of infancy (OpenStax Psychology 2e)
Social beginnings: smiles, babbling, first words (CDC)
Honest framing: infancy as the steepest learning curve in human life
supporting: Milestones as things most children (75% or more) can do by a given age (CDC)
Wide normal variation in milestone timing, including cultural variation (OpenStax Psychology 2e 9.1)
Object permanence as an early sensorimotor achievement
Reflexes present at birth as starting points (MedlinePlus)

claims.claim: Infancy is generally considered the period from birth until about age 2 years, and it is a time of rapid growth and change.
Developmental milestones are things most children (75% or more) can do by a certain age; they are typical ranges with variation, not absolute deadlines.

Timing of motor milestones such as sitting, crawling, and walking varies widely; the average age of first walking is about 12 months, but child-rearing practices and individual differences can shift these ages, so a 14-month-old who has not yet walked can still be within the normal range.

Per CDC's 2022-updated milestone checklists, typical motor firsts include: rolling from tummy to back by about 6 months, sitting without support by about 9 months, pulling up to stand and walking while holding furniture around 12 months, and taking a few steps on one's own around 15 months.

Crawling is a common skill by about 9 months, but it is not universal: CDC's current checklists do not list crawling, and milestone lists such as MedlinePlus's include it among 9-month abilities, so babies who skip crawling are not behind.

Sensory development in infancy: hearing is mature at birth and infants prefer the human voice; touch, taste, and smell are mature at birth; a newborn's vision sees clearly only within about 8 to 12 inches, with color vision developing between 4 and 6 months, and by 2 months infants track moving objects and prefer faces.

Piaget's sensorimotor stage is the first stage of cognitive development, lasting from birth to about 2 years, during which infants experience the world through their senses and actions; object permanence typically develops between about 5 and 8 months.

Social and communication beginnings in infancy: most babies smile in response to faces by about 2 months, babble with repeated syllables such as 'mamamama' by about 9 months, and say their first words such as 'mama' or 'dada' by about 12 months.

Infancy is the steepest learning curve in human life: within roughly 24 months a newborn moves from reflexive responses to independent walking, purposeful sensing, and first words, a density of first-time skills no later period matches.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Crawling's status as a milestone: older milestone lists (and MedlinePlus) include crawling around 9 months, while CDC's 2022-updated checklists omit it entirely.
positions: MedlinePlus lists 'is able to crawl' among 9-month developmental abilities.
CDC's current Learn the Signs. Act Early. checklists do not list crawling among 9-month milestones.
OpenStax notes milestones such as crawling are normative guidelines that vary with culture and child-rearing practice.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents crawling as common but optional: many babies crawl around 6-10 months, some use other moves (bottom shuffling, rolling, scooting), and some skip crawling for pulling up and cruising. No source treats crawling as a required milestone or a deadline.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Age at which babies roll over: older CDC checklists listed rolling at 4 months; the 2022-updated CDC checklists place 'rolls from tummy to back' at 6 months.
positions: CDC 2022-updated 6-month checklist: 'rolls from tummy to back'.
Older editions of the CDC checklist listed rolling among 4-month milestones.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the current (2022-updated) CDC checklist as the reference and frames rolling as typically happening between roughly 4 and 6 months, emphasizing range over exact age.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Infancy's upper boundary: some definitions end infancy at 12 months and call ages 1-2 'toddlerhood,' while others treat the whole first two years as infancy.
positions: NICHD: infancy is generally the period from birth until age 2 years.
Erikson's stage theory (per OpenStax) treats 'infancy (birth to 12 months)' as trust vs. mistrust.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson adopts NICHD's working definition (birth to about age 2) as its primary framing and notes the toddler label in passing, attributing the definition to NICHD.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's claim that infancy is 'a foundational concept in Human Development' with no definition, milestones, or attributed content — the draft contained no sourceable facts.
Draft's implication that the lesson's value is mainly 'organizing information' for college assignments rather than describing the developmental period itself.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with a source-verified definition of infancy (birth to about age 2, per NICHD).
Added motor milestones attributed to CDC's 2022-updated checklists, stated as typical ranges with variation rather than deadlines.
Added crawling with honest framing (common by ~9 months per MedlinePlus; not required by CDC's current checklists).
Added sensory development facts from MedlinePlus (hearing/touch/taste/smell mature at birth; newborn vision 8-12 inches; color vision 4-6 months).
Added Piaget's sensorimotor stage (birth to ~2 years) attributed to OpenStax Psychology 2e 9.2.
Added social beginnings (smiles ~2 months, babbling ~9 months, first words ~12 months) per CDC checklists.
Dropped the draft's vague objectives in favor of objectives tied to the verified content.
Added honest framing of infancy as the steepest learning curve with variation emphasized (no alarm language).
rightsIssues: No rights issues: all six sources are used REFERENCE_ONLY; no source prose is reproduced beyond short factual phrases (e.g., CDC's 'most children (75% or more)'), which are facts rather than creative expression. sourceRecords.notes: Read via the web.archive.org capture of 2024-12-31 (cdc.gov blocks direct fetch). The index page defines milestones as things most children (75% or more) can do by a certain age and links to age-specific pages; specific items were taken from the age pages at the same capture: milestones-2mo.html (smiles when talked to, reacts to loud sounds, looks at your face), milestones-4mo.html (head steady, turns head toward voice, watches you as you move, smiles on his own to get your attention, cooing), milestones-6mo.html (rolls from tummy to back, leans on hands when sitting, puts things in mouth to explore), milestones-9mo.html (sits without support, gets to a sitting position by herself, babbles 'mamamama'/'bababababa'), milestones-1yr.html (pulls up to stand, walks holding on to furniture, calls a parent 'mama'/'dada', understands 'no'), milestones-15mo.html (takes a few steps on his own).

sourceRecords.title: Infant — Newborn Development (Medical Encyclopedia)
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-22. Supports sensory development facts: hearing begins before birth and is mature at birth (infants prefer the human voice); touch, taste, and smell are mature at birth; a newborn sees within a range of 8 to 12 inches; color vision develops between 4 and 6 months; by 2 months infants track moving objects and prefer faces. Also lists newborn primitive reflexes (Moro/startle, grasp, rooting and sucking).
